Taken together, these observations indicate that the GRU offers the best trade-off between accuracy and training efficiency for the dataset and problem formulation used here, with the LSTM providing essentially equivalent accuracy at modest additional cost. To increase confidence in ML-driven inverter emulation and move toward field and real-time deployment, the first priority is to evaluate model robustness under safety-critical conditions. Subsequent experiments should incorpo- rate fault conditions, extreme transients, islanding events and grid disturbances so models can be tested on out-of- distribution behaviours that are most relevant for protection and control. Complementary to this, integrating uncer- tainty quantification and anomaly detection into the modeling pipeline will provide calibrated confidence measures, such as probabilistic outputs and online anomaly detectors, to help define safe fallback behaviours when the ML model encounters unfamiliar operating regimes. Another promising direction is the development of physics-informed ML architectures, combining physics-based fundamentals with observed data to improve extrapolation and to reduce the volume of required training data. Fi- nally, deployment validation through hardware-in-the-loop tests will be critical to demonstrate real-world viability through real-time inference. 9 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
